#4135. Nintendo's Bill Trinen Explains Why Ocarina Of Time Is The Perfect Place To Start In The Zelda Universe

If you're in a position where you've never actually played a Zelda game before, Nintendo's Bill Trinen just wants to let you know Ocarina of Time is the "perfect place" to start.

Although this comment just happens to line up with the arrival of the Switch 2 remake, Nintendo's VP of Player & Product Experience really is convinced this is the best game to begin with, as it's a "foundational story", where the player is taught everything they need to know about the world and characters.

Here's what he had to say at the remake's launch event in San Francisco this week:

Bill Trinen: "This is the perfect place for your first Zelda game, because you are gonna learn everything that there is about the world and the characters that will serve sort of as the foundation for all the others, all the games that came after.

"This game is sort of a really foundational story for the lore of the Legend of Zelda. It really tells the story of Link and his journey becoming a hero. It tells the story of Link and his connection to Zelda and their relationship with Ganondorf. And overall, it communicates kind of what is at the moral core of is all the series, which is the idea that wisdom and courage combined can overcome power."

There will likely be more eyes than ever on the Zelda series in 2027, when the live-action film arrives in cinemas in April. So Ocarina of Time truly is a fantastic entry point into the Zelda universe if you haven't played the games before. The remake on Switch 2 also updates the gameplay and mechanics to offer a more accessible experience.

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

News Nintendo Excited About Broadening Zelda's Audience With Live-Action Movie

"That's one of the most exciting things for us"

What are your thoughts about Bill's comments here? In terms of Ocarina's story and universe, do you think it's the perfect entry point into the Zelda series, or would you recommend starting with something else? Let us know in the comments.

Liam is a news writer and reviewer on Nintendo Life. He's been writing about games for more than 15 years and is a lifelong fan of many iconic video game characters.

I mean it's a prequel that provides the framework for every game that comes after it, it's one of the earliest games in the series, it's pretty much the only 3D game that doesn't really have one massive unique quirk that dominates the game's structure and is just pick-up-and-play, and the only games set before it are two highly experimental side things that are still heavily rooted in the plots of other games, it'd be weird if it wasn't the best entry point at least on the 3D side.

2D though I'd probably say the best place to start is the Link's Awakening remake? It's not my favorite 2D one - Link Between Worlds is - but Link's Awakening is where a lot of the series structure first really came into being, I think it's a more tightly designed experience than LttP is (not sure which I actually prefer but LttP definitely has some early growing pains with some of its choices), and the Switch version has some handy conveniences like keeping the sword equipped that the GB version lacks.

And IS what Zelda games are supposed to be.

Couldn't agree more and as already mentioned here another reason is that most Zelda games after Ocarina and before Breath of the Wild are based on this game in some way or the other - anyway, hope those playing Ocarina for the first time thanks to the remake have fun (personally I'm absolutely loving it as someone who has played several previous versions)!

The only issue is that the only way is down from the gaming perfection that is Ocarina.

Glad you hold Ocarina in such a high regard, Jey. At the time it didn’t fully stick the landing for me, but I am hopeful this version will make me a bigger fan - I know the start was way more convincing for me this time around than back in 1998! Crossing fingers that’s how I will feel throughout :3 (BotW / LttP and the original are my favs before playing this, let’s see if that has changed when I’m finished!)

I certainly agree that Ocarina is and always has been the best entry point to the series. It's interesting that Bill says that the moral of the series is that courage and wisdom combined can overcome power. To me, Link's heroics across all the games has always seemed to be framed as a mastery of all three, which is why he's the hero chosen by the Gods, rather than Farore alone. It will be interesting to see if this comment gives a clue to some ideas which will be explored in the movie next year.

Honestly, there’s a lot of Zelda games that are a good entry point. The OG game (this is where I started), OoT, Windwaker, BotW, Link’s Awakening, etc… I mean, as long as you’re not starting with the GBA or DS spin-off games that focused on gimmicky mechanics, you’ve got a good starting point.

It certainly has a few advantages; it's not too long/large, and the remake definitely streamlined the experience making it very welcoming to newcomers. It's also less abstruse than say The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild could be a good contender though, despite the long overall length of the average playthrough.

It’s silly for Nintendo to use terms like “entry points” now for particular games it goes against everything they’ve ever done, it’s a word the rest of the industry uses to make their games appear more approachable, I hilariously recall EA using it a lot for Mass Effect 3. Nintendo’s whole entire deal is making anything they develop be entry points.

"This game is sort of a really foundational story for the lore of Super Mario Bros. It really tells the story of Mario and his journey saving the princess. It tells the story of Mario and his connection to Peach and their relationship with Bowser. And overall, it communicates kind of what is at the moral core of is [sic] all the series, which is the idea that if Bowser kidnaps the princess, Mario must save her."

I certainly agree that Ocarina of Time is a great series entry point. It's a great example of the classic formula and lays the foundations for a lot of characters and themes that appear throughout the series.

However, it's far from the only great entry point. Some games certainly fit this more than others; I wouldn't encourage playing clearly direct sequels or some of the more difficult/obscure entries first (Looking at you, Zelda II). My entry point was Twilight Princess on the Wii, and I've loved the series ever since. And have played/beaten every mainline entry in some form except Four Swords Adventures since it's still GameCube locked.

We are playing this new version (only the appropriate parts of course!) together with our 4-year-olds and they are absolutely captivated, it's so sweet.

I don't show them any combat or monsters at all, just places and NPC's and stuff, and just a short session at a time.

This is going to leave an impression on them for sure, they love it. I didn't think I'd have any use for the preorder bonus (the 3 "Spiritual Stones"), now they currently take them everywhere they go.

Back in the 90s OOT was my entry into the series. I was a SEGA kid, so the N64 was my first Nintendo console (other than the Game Boy). I was aware of the games, mainly from the cheesy cartoon and a quick go on the original game at friends’ houses, but Ocarina got me hooked. My young daughter has been watching her brother playing and it seems have ‘clicked’ for her, where BOTW failed to.

It is a perfect first game that encourages exploration but is never so big that you can get lost. The story is simple and it introduces many of the series key ideas and themes.

The issue I have always found is that in the 28 years since of first played it, no other Zelda game has had the same impact! I have loved several others (Wind Waker, Majora’s mask, link between worlds) and played them all, but nothing has ever quite clicked like OOT (though Echoes of Wisdom I am very fond of).

"We just spent a lot of money putting shiny graphics on a game that was previously free to play, so it makes sense for new players to buy it. Because money!"-Company

A Link to the Past really deserves some love in this conversation, too. It may not have the cinematic story stuff going for it, but it absolutely perfected the experience of playing a Legend of Zelda game. It’s an old game, but the sprite work and art design are gorgeous, and it’s very playable by today’s standards, more so than Ocarina (N64) I think. Fantastic exploration and secrets, really good dungeons, and a whimsical but a bit dark atmosphere. It’s the gold standard for top-down, search-action-RPGs. It’s a phenomenal game, and the one I have the most connection to, from an emotional perspective. Surprised to see it getting mentioned less and less these days when Legend of Zelda comes up in conversation.

I wonder if perhaps A Link to the Past may be next for the remake treatment… I’d love to see it remade in the diorama style. Hmm…

I think OoT is a good point to start at because it's an accumulation point of what Zelda had been up to that point, and lays the framework for what Zelda would be moving forward. Besides that, it's just a classic tale in general that's easy to understand. I'm sure it'll be the biggest inspiration for the movie.

@Aquinas Ocarina of Time was never legally free to play.

I mean, to the extent that there is an overarching plot, Ocarina of Time is probably a good one if you're trying to keep a mental continuity, fool's errand it may be. It also is one of the games that really sets out "big ideas" of what the series could be.

If you're interested in the latter rationale, I think A Link to the Past, which actually did allow for a lot of sequence breaking, or Breath of the Wild are other good options that we would consider friendly to those that may not have patience with the more iterative entries' quirks. I also have a soft spot for Link's Awakening as the first one where nearly everyone in the world is just really weird in a non-threatening Twin Peaks kinda way.

But in any case, tell your friends to play some Zelda!

He is right about the foundational aspect. OoT really focused on building a mythos that both NoA and NoJ/HQ agreed on so if somebody is like “what is LoZ”, OoT is probably the best place to start. Skyward Sword might be next but it is more lore heavy I feel. OoT gives you an easy to digest overview that then you can branch out from.

The TV adaptation is apparently still moving forward

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The headwinds of the industry led to the closure of BioWare recently, and the latent Mass Effect 5 – known internally as Mass Effect Universe – went with it. We may never know exactly what the devs were putting together for the sequel, but details are dripping out, the latest being that it would've tied into the planned Amazon TV show in some way.

Michael Gamble, former project director and executive producer at BioWare, addresses a fan on Twitter asking if the Mass Effect Universe plot would be used for the show. "Both are meant to compliment each other," he responds.

That's a fascinating wrinkle. It seems like the two productions were collaborating together to some degree, if only to keep each other informed of their narrative intentions. Among the other titbits we've learned about the fifth Mass Effect is the notion that it would've involved a multiverse.

According to Gamble the plot from Mass Effect Universe and the TV show were supposed to compliment each other. If the show is still happening this may be our only hope #SaveMassEffect https://t.co/hY7pQtcA0zNovember 8, 2026

Apparently you would've been able to jump across timelines somehow. The exact mechanics for how are unknown, but on top of anything else, this means every possible outcome from the original trilogy is technically canon. Clever, because I lowkey dreaded seeing the discourse tear itself open once everyone saw which of the endings from Mass Effect 3 BioWare favored.

Details of what's going on with the TV adaptation are scant. Amazon and MGM announced the production back in 2024, and progress has been slow since. However, reports have emerged that it's still on the docket and moving forward, with showrunners Doug Jung and Daniel Casey in tow.

When we see it is anyone's guess. Thankfully, we're at a point where many video game adaptations have proven lucrative, which means the likelihood this quietly disappears is smaller. Gamble's comment is being shared around with the idea that gives hope to saving Mass Effect.

I'm not sure about that, but at least the franchise will live on in some form. It's ironic really, since one of the reasons I fell in love with the first game is that it felt like the Star Trek RPG I hadn't gotten before. Now it might just be the new Star Trek show I've been yearning for.

Playing mouse pi, monster hunter stories 3 and look outside.

This weekend I started a game everyone Recognizes

One of many Sony exclusives that I needed to finally try. I've only been playing for a couple of hours and so far my impressions are beyond brilliant. I've gone hunting with the boy, taken a giant stone totem to the face from a troll, punched a man (who wouldn't shut up) through a mountain, thrown him down into the depths of who knows where and even done some flower picking. The story so far feels really special, the bond between Father and son isn't something I get to see in the kind of games I usually play and not being solo makes the journey that much more interesting.

I really like throwing the axe at monsters, the feel of Kratos's raw unrestrained rage as he pounds on things with his big fists, and all while the score booms and echoes in my eardrums. The voice acting is fantastic too, Christopher Judge sounds so intense and gravely, he was made for the role. His delivery is flawless, I wish I could say the same for my combat skills but circle not being dodge is tricky to adjust to. The upgrade system is satisfying, the environments aren't too big or too small. I can't imagine how much of a leap forward it must have been on PS4. The combat is very responsive, everything looks sharp, the textures like skin and fabric really pop, and the vistas themselves are stunning. It's going to be a busy weekend though so the chances of finishing the game so soon are unlikely. Then there's my newest Steamdeck game, my other travel companion.

It's a store simulator with a difference. The aesthetic is similar to Coffee Talk. At night you scavenge for junk and trinkets then during the day you try to flog them to whoever happens to drop by. Other scavengers try to sell and barter/scam you. All manner of gypsys, tramps and thieves make up the customer base and the humour is great too. You can turn wanted felons in for reward money, learn to appraise items for some extra easy money, fleece tourists, or opt out of contraband completely and try to run an above board business (not happening) The upgrade system is the best I've seen in the genre. It's not on console and it needs to be. I also finished The Midnight Walk and loved every minute of it, the story was so moving, the score is now a favourite and the sculpting was so unique. So that's about it really I think Kratos will be good company for a couple of days, Tuesday I'll be surviving Warhammer style and doing something raccoon related to a coin machine for yet even more dopamine doses.

@old_gamer74 Oh brilliant, it definitely does some really unique and special things. For such a short playthrough there's nothing to lose but a couple of hours. My best advice for The Witcher 3 is to stick with it, I was overwhelmed and lost with the story too and the more I played the more sense it made. Combat gets easier and flows better the more geared you become, if you run into trouble with Gwent buy spy cards from vendors and play as the Northern Realms. They make Gwent easier and Quen (shield) will make combat easier until you get your rotations down. Parry humans, dodge monsters, I didn't roll much it drains stamina. The bestiary was one of my biggest boons, it explains how to defeat the various enemies. You'll earn more by selling weapons to blacksmiths, armor to armorer. Sometimes dismantle is better than selling, example shells into pearls, it's a higher markup. Also get the DLC if you haven't already, it's some of the best DLCs of any game.

@naruball I experienced the same thing with the game. The first couple of times I played I kept getting overrun by zombies and struggled to clear even one map. I think my favorite feature is that while you can upgrade stats for the whole character roster, you can upgrade each character solo too and they get really strong. My favorite combination was the Mercenary, Medic and Shotgun man. It gets so satisfying when endless mode is unlocked and the confidence is there to just go for it. I think my longest run was three-hours, I had a podcast playing and they were doing all of the heavy lifting.

#4132. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.8 is refreshing your team comps with a new mechanic, and the game is coming to Steam

Zenless Zone Zero will soon become the first HoYoverse game to make its way to Steam, though we wish we had more details.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a pretty exciting Zenless Zone Zero Special Program that not only delivered all the details on the next big update, it also came with the unexpected announcement that the action RPG is on its way to Steam.

Previously, all HoYoverse games with PC versions have always been directly available from the developer’s website, or through the Epic Games Store. In other words, Zenless Zone Zero will soon mark the massive company’s debut on Valve’s platform.

The main focus of the livestream, of course, has been Version 2.8, otherwise known as New Eridan Sunset. This upcoming release is scheduled for May 6, though the Steam version does not yet have a date.The new release sees the release of two new Agents, as well as the brand-new Wind attribute enemy.

The release also acts as the last chapter of Season 2, and it sees Ramiel becoming the main target of different factions in the Outer Ring. The two new arrivals, together with Proxies and Cissia will embark on a quest to learn the new identity of Ramiel.

The first new Agent is Promeia, the executioner of Krampus. She’s an S-Rank Ice Anomaly Agent who can consume Trial by Cold to trigger Abloom on enemies. This is done by converting Corrosive Chill.

By using her EX Special Attack, she can enter the Bound Absolution state, which allows her to automatically Perfect Dodge any attack that targets her. If you have another Anomaly or Support Agent on the team, Promeia can further boost the entire squad’s Abloom damage.

The second addition in 2.8 is Starlight - Billy, also an S-Rank Agent, though wielding Physical Rupture instead. This is the upgraded form of Billy, and he arrives on a combat motorcycle to bring his signature Starlight Knight to the fight. Through it, he can deliver big Physical burst damage.

The higher Billy’s health, the more Sheer damage he deals. In fact, all Physical damage he deals lands as Sheer damage. Further building on his tank-like role, his skills can also restore his own health.

Re-runs in Version 2.8 will be Lucia in the first half, and Orphie & Magus in the second. The other exciting addition coming with this update is the new Wind attribute enemy, and the accompanying Vortex mechanic.

When an enemy is inflicted with the Wind Attribute Anomaly, any other Anomaly attack type that gets applied will trigger Vortex, rather than Disorder. This deals AoE Anomaly damage of the type that matches the corresponding element.

Throughout the version’s runtime, you’ll be able to take part in the Marcel Bootopia-themed event, which gives you control of Eous and lets you explore a Bangboo resort island. The island has been closed due to an outbreak of Hollows, and you must rescue Bangboos and find treasures.

If you do, you’ll earn Booltergeist and its Bangboo core for your troubles. This is an A-Rank Bangboo that can float around and fire lasers in combat. Its damage is further boosted whenever certain teammates are present.

The Ultimate Verdict Trial is another event you can check out that lets you fight alongside newcomer Promeia, or take part in other mini-activities that all reward Polychrome. Finally, you can look forward to a new Hoshimi Miyabi outfit: Dignified Blossom, which will be available in the store.

Before you jump back in next month, it always helps to catch up on the latest Zenless Zone Zero codes to make sure you’re not missing out on any freebies.

The model will apparently be "hatching soon"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new Lego Yoshi set is on the way, and based on a few clues, it seems as though it'll be a big one.

Teased via the Nintendo Today app (which provides personalized updates for you based on the games you like), the Lego Yoshi set appears in an extreme close up with the promise that it's "hatching soon." Because this is a for-adults model, it'll be a display piece - presumably a full figure - rather than a playset like the upcoming 2027 range. Some of the best Lego sets so far have been Super Mario collector's items, so the bar is pretty high here.

All we can see of the new kit is its face, with eyes and part of a nose poking out the side of the screen. However, it's possible to guess how large Yoshi will be by the size of the pieces on display... and from what I can tell, it'll be to scale with the Mario and Standard Kart set (which may tell us something about price, because that one's currently $150 on Amazon). The curved pieces with a single stud on the nose are around an inch across at the widest point, for example, so Yoshi's head looks as though it'll be roughly four inches tall. You can then start to work backwards and figure out how big the rest of the model will be.

Using that guestimate and assuming he's standing, I suspect he'll be around a foot or so as a result - e.g. a similar size or just taller than the Lego Piranha Plant set (which used those same curved pieces for its head), but smaller than Lego The Mighty Bowser.

Naturally, all this assumes he isn't on a vehicle like Lego Luigi & Mach 8. If he is, that'll obviously change things because he's sat rather than standing proud. I'm not sure what they'd put him on, but he's often seen on bikes in Mario Kart 8 or the Wild Wiggler kart. Because we've seen a couple of karts already courtesy of Mario and Luigi, I'd quite like to see the franchise's bikes get some love this time around.

First discovered by Vooks, this is a slightly unusual way for Lego to unveil a new set; at the time of writing, you can only find it on the Nintendo Today app. Still, that tease does give us some handy information nonetheless. Judging by the 2027 trademark we know for a fact Lego Yoshi won't be launching this year, for instance.

Even if he doesn't cross the finish line until later, it's still a good time to be a fan of Lego dinosaurs right now; alongside Yoshi, a huge Lego Godzilla kit was revealed last week. While it's changed a lot since the original fan design was submitted, it's still tremendously impressive. Hopefully Yoshi will live up to that.

It's unclear how much this kit will be, but we do know plenty of models will get a big price cut for the 2026 Black Friday Lego deals.

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

#4130. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (November 7-8)

Anything you need to complete before...y'know?

Just two more weekends to get stuck into the games you're likely to abandon come November 19th.

It's been a fairly chill week for new releases with ZERO PARADES: Director's Cut the only notable launch (at least in my opinion). Hopefully something from our Deep Discounts sales roundup, or Xbox's Free Play Days titles are worth a shot.

Alrighty then, let's get into it. Here's what we're playing on Xbox this weekend:

I think I'm in need of a nice, feel good weekend of gaming. I'd like to play stuff that leaves me feeling all warm and fuzzy. It's appropriate timing, really, considering just how quickly it's getting dark now that the clocks have changed here in the UK.

Top of the agenda is starting The Wolf Among Us Remastered. I claimed the original version with Games with Gold, yet I've still not managed to boot it. Somehow, I've managed to avoid all spoilers in the thirteen year stretch. All I know is there's a pig called Colin or something. Anyway, I'm very excited to finally play it, as I've only ever heard good things about it.

Another game I'd like to experience for the first time is It Takes Two. My lady love and I are looking for our next co-op adventure after completing Split Fiction, so what better choice than Hazelight's other phenomenal game?

Oh, and if I get time, I'd also like to check out Routine. It isn't exactly giving warm and cosy vibes, but I'm worried it could leave Xbox Game Pass soon, and with GTA 6 on the horizon I don't have spare funds floating around.

I've got quite a lot going on this weekend, so I don't expect to be playing too much. Hopefully I might be able to fit in some more Star Wars Galactic Racer and Tape to Tape though - both of those games are so incredible!

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade on Xbox Game Pass is also something I'm planning to spend a lot of time with, possibly when I go on holiday in a few weeks' time. I played the demo and loved it, so now it's time to try the full thing!

#4129. Feature: Box Art Brawl: The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Ultimate Showdown

Welcome all, to a very special edition of Box Art Brawl!

Looking back at last week, we checked out Revenge of the 'Gator to celebrate its addition to Nintendo Switch Online. Both designs for this one are great in their own way, but it was Japan that took home the trophy with 58% of the vote, leaving North America and Europe to mop up the remaining 42%.

This week, we're doing something special. We've already covered the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the N64 along with the 2011 3DS remake. However, with the release of the Switch 2 remake, we thought we'd throw every box art into the ring for an ultimate showdown.

You'll note that we haven't included every Ocarina of Time release here. The bonus disc included with Wind Waker pre-orders for the GameCube also included the logo for Master Quest, so we're not adding it here. Similarly, the Collector's Edition disc for GameCube had no direct reference to Ocarina of Time on its box art, so it too has been excluded.

So with that said, let's get cracking, hm?

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

Round Up The Reviews Are In For The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time On Switch 2

Feature Song Of Time - Every Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Release, From N64 To Switch 2

This is the classic box art, right? The one of which most of you will likely be familiar. It's simple yet effective, with the game's iconic logo presented against a plain gold background. Chef's kiss. Did it really need anything else? Probably not, and it served as a wonderful thematic continuation of A Link to the Past.

Europe's design is equally simple, yet equally stunning. This time, we have a jet black background punctuated by a shining gold logo in the centre. In fact, all of the text here is in gold. Again, it's the simplicity that really sells it, and the contrast to the North American version is particularly striking.

Japan's N64 approach is very cool. It utilises the portrait orientation to great effect, showcasing an image of Link riding Epona, while flames surround the outside of the composition. There's a bit more going on here compared to the western designs, but there's still a sense of simplicity with the approach. It's not busy at all, and we love the contrast of the black and white background against the coloured logo.

The North American approach for the 3DS takes the same image of Link and Epona from the original Japanese release. It also leans heavily on that classic gold presentation, resulting in a classy yet eye-catching final image.

This here is the winner of our Ocarina of Time 3D brawl, and it's easy to see why. We can see Link and Epona depicted over on the right, but your eyes are just immediately drawn to the stunning landscape of Hyrule Field. Lon Lon Ranch, Hyrule Castle, and Death Mountain are all visible, and it's just such a stunning interpretation of the game's most iconic environments.

Okay, finally we have the box art for the latest release on Switch 2, and holy moly, it's absolutely gorgeous. Many folks will have picked up the textured foil version, and this just adds a whole new layer to its beauty. Interestingly, this is the only box art to feature Child Link, but it's a nice approach. It really delivers that sense of whimsy and adventure you feel during those opening portions of the game, and it's just such an impactful composition. Lovely stuff. Changing the logo text to gold is a nice touch too.

Guide Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Walkthrough (Switch 2 Remake): Guide To The Main Quest, Side Quests & Collectables

Thank you for voting! We'll see you next week for another edition of Box Art Brawl!

Nintendo Life’s resident horror fanatic, when he’s not knee-deep in Resident Evil and Silent Hill lore, Ollie likes to dive into a good horror book while nursing a lovely cup of tea. He also enjoys long walks and listens to everything from TOOL to Chuck Berry.

Definitely going with the European / Japanese 3DS one. Switch 2 one's also solid, the others are all very dull. Really never at all cared for the plain gold Zelda covers and glad that trend eventually died.

I still think the golden one is a classic and gives you an entry point view that you’re getting into something truly special.

My favorite is the North America 3DS box art. I don’t have any real deep reason for it beyond just liking the aesthetic of it. I feel pretty indifferent towards the Europe/Japan 3DS box art and Switch 2 box art.

NS2 for putting child Link on it. 3DS JP comes close second, but its decentralised placements make it look like they just slapped the logo on a (beautiful) artwork. Otoh, decentralised artwork is its own spice…

I will never understand why people like the bland AF western boxes for the N64 version. Japan isn't great, mind, but at least it's not just text.

The Switch 2 cover is easily the best one. Really catches that fairy tale vibe.

If you look closely at the 3DS EU one, you can see that one of the birds is actually Kaepora Gaebora.

Definitely going for one of the box arts that show some characters and the setting (the non-Japanese N64 box arts are too generic, they could be for any Zelda game), in particular 3DS - Europe/Japan - I'm also a big fan of the Switch 2 one and it looks gorgeous, but the former shows more characters and locations, plus it's reminiscent of the title screen!

Thinking about it, the golden font is a nice save, NS2 boxes already have more than enough red as is.

I'm just now noticing that the NA 64 box is stretching the logo vertically. Heads would be rolling nowadays.

It's between SW2 and EU/JP 3DS. I chose the EU/JP 3DS boxart because it shows more of Hyrule than just Kokiri Forest. SW2 does get point for it shiny foil. Just being a background color plus logo is really boring. NA 3DS does add some artwork but it just doesn't look that good.

#4128. Genshin Impact Luna 7 brings us the first playable Hexenzirkel as things take a turn in Sumeru

Genshin Impact's Luna 7 update will kick off a new Archon Quest chapter, and deliver some interesting new additions to the playable roster.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a new Genshin Impact Special Program, where the developer revealed everything there is to know about the game’s next major update. Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, or as its friends call it, Luna 7, was unveiled as part of the showcase.

This next update has a lot going for it, and it will be in players’ hands everywhere on May 20.

Luna 7 will take us back to Sumeru for its new Archon Quest, where a new crisis that threatens to plunge the nation into chaos is brewing. Nahida is out of the picture, and someone who looks suspiciously like Il Dottore has emerged.

If you complete this chapter at launch, you’ll earn up to 560 Primogems, as well as Nicole's Ascension Materials. Nicole is the first of three playable characters arriving with this update. Something else you’ll unlock if you finish the chapter quickly is a new Weekly Boss that HoYo says has “unpredictable abilities.”

And if you haven’t played in a while, don’t worry, you can refer to the Guiding Notes feature to catch you up on what’s been going on in the world. This is part of a larger effort from the team to make story progression more seamless, and also includes improved quest autosave prompts.

Nicole Reeyn is highest-profile and most interesting, being the first playable member of the Hexenzirkel. The mage is a 5-Star Pyro Catalyst wielder intended as a support member of the team. She can boost the ATK of all party members, even those not currently on the field. She also generates a shield while doing so.

Her Elemental Burst allows her to summon an Arcane Projection that follows the active character, sending out Coordinated Attacks that match their Elemental Type. Outside of combat, Nicole can help you find treasures by calling upon a Seelie to guide you to them. Quite fitting, as you’ll be exploring in the inside of the Witch's Lodge in Nicole’s Meeting Point in Luna 7, so bring her along.

Lohen, the Vice Captain of the Knights of Favonius' Fifth Company, is the second new character. Also a 5-Star addition, he is instead a Cryo Polearm wielder designed for aggressive combat. His main use is dealing massive Cryo DMG, and he can do that by managing two resources unique to him: Joy, and Will to Win.

Through his Elemental Skill, he can enter the Masterstroke state, allowing him to build up (and consume) Joy to unleash enhanced skills. The more his teammates fight, the more Will to Win he biulds, which can later be used to boost his effectiveness further. For an even more powerful display of force, bring along a Hexerei character when he’s on your team.

Prune is the third and final addition. Prune is a 4-Star Anemo Catalyst wielder, and her kit is inspired by her Witch Hunter aspirations. Using a bell and a hammer, she can deal DMG of several elements at once, and trigger Swirl reactions.

Nicole, and Lohen will debut in Luna 7’s first half, while Prune will follow in the second. The first half will also see a Durin rerun, with Mavuika returning in the second half. You can look forward to a new limited-time event as part of Luna 7, with a focus on Klee's Little Hexenzirkel.

You’ll find a series of mini-games you can play alongside Prune, as well as Qiqi, Yaoyao, and Sayu. If you play, you could earn the Super Awesome Magic Key, an exclusive weapon skin. Miliastra Wonderland is doing its thing, too, with a new sports festival for you to take part in.

One new gameplay addition worth calling attention to is that Manekins can now perform actions in Teyvat. The Kamera, which you can use to capture moments with Manekins, is getting upgraded, too, with new editing tools and assets.

Before you pick the game back up, be sure to check out our recently-updated Genshin Impact codes page for some free stuff you may be missing.

#4127. GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo

Images of GTA 6’s physical edition have emerged on Reddit, ahead of its release later in the month.

The anticipated open world game – which won’t include a disc – looks practically identical to every other PS5 release, in a sealed blue plastic case with the usual logos and layout.

While this is a German copy, there’s a disclaimer on the front which mentions no disc is included, and only a download code is packaged inside.

The photos, first shared on Reddit but since deleted, have been reposted below:

Fans will be able to purchase boxed versions of the Rockstar release from retailers starting 12th November, allowing a week for them to pre-load the 212GB title ahead of launch.

This is the first major title to ship in a “code-in-box” format, although it will become a lot more common in 2028, when Sony’s signalled its intent to cease manufacturing Blu-ray discs.

Personally, I’m concerned about the waste of plastic here. I understand some people may still want a case to display with their other games, but if we’re getting rid of discs, I’d like Sony to implement some sort of recyclable format moving forward.

Remember, if you want a map of Leonidas to go with your physical copy of GTA 6, you’ll need to purchase that separately for $0.99 from the Rockstar Store.

You can find out more information about GTA 6’s pre-load through here.

In the meantime, do let me know if any of you are planning to purchase the physical version and why below.

At extreme ends of the spectrum game streaming could be the best for the environment if you were just trialling a massive game file for a short amount of time - it has its place - but became significantly worse the longer you played. (Good for AAA demos) Streaming was also the worst for the environment in cases where you were streaming tiny games for a longer time. It’s why I refuse to use Antstream Arcade which is streaming retro game files that are often measured in kilobytes, or perhaps megabytes and using hundreds or thousands of times that data throughput every minute.

For physical and digital media you are right the game size affects how effecient this is, and there is a tipping point somewhere in the middle, however studies varied wildly about where this was and with so many assumptions and simplifications taken it’s hard to say with any certainty what is right.

If you want to read more Eurogamer did a massive deep dive into these studies a few years ago as part of Earth week. You can find them on google. Just take all the results with a massive pinch of salt. The only conclusion I got was that there was no final conclusion.

#4126. New PS Portal announced for Japan, with a mysterious storage upgrade to support "future functionality"

Sony has updated the PlayStation Portal in Japan, releasing a new handheld that maintains many of the same features as the original, with one key difference. The revised gaming handheld now includes internal storage.

That signals a big shift away from the brand's original vision for the device. The PS Portal we know in the US and UK functions as a remote player first and foremost, streaming PS5 games from a console (or separately via a PlayStation Plus Premium account). It's still one of the best PS5 accessories, but with the PS6 expected to launch alongside its own handheld device, there's one line in Sony's official announcement that brings this internal storage under the microscope.

"With an eye towards future functionality," the PlayStation Japan blog post states, "the new model includes additional internal storage."

It's that future functionality that has ears pricked across the industry this morning. Sony states that more information on this mysterious storage is incoming, with details surrounding the feature still to be "finalized." However, it's one of the first official statements we've had linking Sony's current lineup to its future handheld ambitions.

What that storage will be used for in the existing PS Portal remains a mystery. With no listed upgrades to the internals, it would be pretty difficult to consider Sony running games directly from the Portal handheld in its current state. We also don't know how much extra storage is under the hood.

Just after launch, it was discovered that the existing PlayStation Portal has 6GB of free space floating around. Including the storage upgrade within the announcement, and citing future features, makes it seem like there's a chunkier drive being added - rather than a few extra gigs to support a larger Android OS update.

The new PlayStation Portal launches in Japan only and, like the Midnight Black PS5 announced last month, it's pretty locked down to the region. It can only be set to Japanese language and requires a Japanese PSN account to run. That said, it will be available to pre-order in the region from November 13, at the same ¥39,980 price as the regular model.

#4125. Mystic Messenger's most loyal players are getting banned in droves for seemingly playing the game too much

With the 10th anniversary of Mystic Messenger nearly upon us, the dating sim has inexplicably begun issuing wide-spread bans for its most active players.

Mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years. Despite not receiving new content or any meaningful updates in all that time, the game remains popular with its core fans, many of whom just woke up to some shocking news about their accounts.

The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts. So far, it looks like players with 1,000 or more have been targeted, but others with far fewer hoards have reported getting the axe, too.

The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.

The message players received is identical, and doesn’t mention the specific reason for the ban. “Your account has been banned because abusive behavior has been detected from your account,” it reads, ending with a support email address the affected user can contact if they believe they’d banned in error.

It didn’t take a while for players to realise that most, if not all of the bans are for players with thousands of Hourglasses in their accounts. The virtual currency can both be acquired in-game just by playing, as well as through direct real-money purchases.

For a nearly ten-year-old game that stopped receiving content three years into its life, it’s easy to see how a dedicated group of players would be able to acquire so many Hourglasses by simply playing regularly for so long.

When contacted by the affected players, Cheritz, the developer and publisher of the game, has instructed them to send receipts of how they acquired Hourglasses (assuming they were purchased) to verify whether or not they’d been fraudulently obtained.

Considering that Mystic Messenger has practically been abandoned by its developer, certain exploits have emerged over the years that allowed players to farm Hourglasses faster than intended, but those instances have always been dealt with then and there.

The blanket and sudden nature of this ban is what’s spooked players, especially those who’ve been logging in for years and never thought accruing in-game currency from playing the game too much would make them the target of a ban.

The running theory is that most of the bans are unintentional, and may be the result of a new automated security system that’s been implemented. It’s entirely possible, especially if its’s AI-based, that the new system simply couldn’t distinguish between those who have earned (or bought) their Hourglasses fairly, and those who used exploits.

The timing of the ban wave is also suspect. With the game’s 10th anniversary coming up in July, it could be that Cheriz is preparing to release a large update for Mystic Messenger, which may include new content. If most of the playerbase is already sitting on massive amounts of in-game currency, they may simply use that to fast-track their way to unlocking the new content, which would greatly affect the developer’s bottom line.

This is a problem that other live service games have run into in the past. Just recently, extraction shooter Arc Raiders added a cap to the amount of Cred players can hold in their accounts very quickly after its launch. That currency is used to buy cosmetic sets in the store, so the logic is easy to follow.

All of that has certainly put a damper on the enthusiasm of the game’s most active players, many of whom were excited to get together in person for the coming 10th anniversary, participate in community nights and so on to celebrate.

It’s also disheartening to see a fanbase so loyal; playing a game as regularly for so long without new content, to be treated so poorly. Even without knowing what the game is, it’s impressive that so many people have kept the flag of their favourite game flying for so long.

I played the original Football Manger games when they first came out on a very basic PC (as they were back then), and played them for hours upon hours. I absolutely loved them. Something tells me I might have had the game on my ZX Spectrum too in the early 80s, but that might be my memory playing havoc with me as it often does these days, though in fairness, I am thinking back to over 40 years ago!

Anyway, seeing Football Manager 27 coming to Game Pass in the next few days does give me the urge to give it ago to see if I can rekindle some old and fond memories. It would also then be the very first game I have played on Game Pass this year, which would be a bonus...!

Let's see...40 years ago, I bought my first computer - a Commodore 128. It was most useful for the Go64 command, which put it in C64 mode, to run all those games. My favorite was the original Loderunner. My first video game system was the original VCS though, much earlier. I can actually remember visiting friends' houses and playing their Pong systems, which if memory serves correctly (like your memory FB - not so well) was a Magnavox system. My favorite computer was the Amiga, purchased back in around 1987...and 1988, and later but I don't remember when. I owned the 1000, 500, 2000 and 3000 systems at one time or another. My fondest, early, video game event was turning over 1M points in Asteroids (VCS), and quitting about 500K points later, because I was getting tired and bored. Anyway, what was your earliest memories @Fiendish-Beaver ?

My earliest memory of gaming is the first time I ever encountered it, @Droopy. My Father died when I was 6 weeks old in January of 1964, and my Mother raised me alone. However, as my Mother worked, each Summer holiday, I would be dispatched to my Aunts and Uncles who lived about 200 miles North of where I lived, and I would spend 6 weeks in the company of my Cousins.

In the Summer of 1973, at the age of 10, I went to my Cousins as was customary, to find that they had a games machine that played Pong (to my recollection, that is all it played although that might be the only game they had) and I played the game as much as my Cousins would tolerate for the entire 6 weeks. Obviously, they were far better at it than me, but that did not stop hours and hours of fun. It's probably difficult to imagine now, but think what it must have been like to go from never having heard of gaming, to encountering it for the first time. It was mind blowing to 10 year old me! By the end of the holiday, I was absolutely hooked.

The first console that I owned myself was an Intellivision console that I bought in 1982 with money that I earned working for British Sugar stacking huge sacks of er, well... sugar! The sacks weighed almost as much as I did, which as I weighed less than 10 stone at the time probably isn't that much, but the work paid really well. Whilst I do not remember how many games I had for it, one does stick out, and that was Tron Deadly Discs. It was very basic, but you simply had to throw discs to destroy the robots within an arena, and you could enter doors that would sort of teleport you around the arena. I always remember the game because of one night where I just didn't seem capable of dying, and because you could not save the game (and I'm not sure you could pause it either) I just kept playing until something like 4 a.m. even though I had to be up at 6 to go to work! That night I got my highest ever score in the game, and also formed probably one of my fondest memories in gaming too. It just felt epic! I imagine these days, faced with the same game, I'd be bored inside an hour, but back then, it felt like the hight of entertainment.

Effectively, I have been gaming for about 53 years now, and owned at least one console since the age of 18. I've owned an Intellivision console, a Sinclair ZX Spectrum, various Amstrad computers, various Commodore consoles, various Nintendo's, various Sega's, each of the PlayStation and Xbox consoles, and a gaming PC.

I injured my back in 1990/1, and it became increasingly bad as time progressed to the point that I had to medically retire from the Police in 2010. Fortunately, my time in Bomb Disposal and the Police meant that I was able to retire with a reasonable pension, and whilst I have not been able to work for the past 16 years, I have been able to game every day since, so injuring my back has had it's upsides even if I cannot walk particularly well or far! So, every cloud and what have you... 😉

Thanks for posting @Fiendish-Beaver ! I always enjoy reading your posts, whether here or on Push Square's comments sections. I think I actually read more of Pure XBox's comments sections than I do Push Square's, so I miss some Push Square comments' posts. Frankly, I enjoy the users more here, although there is some caustic ones here as well...and some familiar ones as well! Anyway, yeah my mom bought me my first Atari VCS, better known as the Atari 2600...as far as I remember, one of the more loving things she did for me. She felt sorry for me missing out. I couldn't always borrow my older brother's unit. What a cool thing to have happen to a child! She's no longer with us, but I still love her for it. I suppose parents buying their child a video game system is common now, what with all the pricing(!). But it was really special back then...especially for me. I can't remember the year - had to be 197x when it happened. Not sure! Kudos to all parents for buying their kids video game systems. In the language of the 70's, that is really cool! I got a loving wife now, that lets me buy whatever floats in my imagination. That's really cool too! You don't find something like that...well, at all in a lot of people's cases. But, I found one! Of course, I married her because she had a good heart. What profound wisdom was I reading at the time? It's worth more than gold to me! You can't buy people that really love you. And we play couch coop nearly every week. Borderlands 4, Serious Sam, Gears (All of them!). I've got the latest Gears (forget what it's called, oh yeah Eday (Emergence Day)), we haven't bothered to even play it yet! LOL We'll love it when we do - we finished all the others, several times, and loved them. Where can you get a wife that is happy when you're happy, and loves video games? Ah well, some thing's are priceless. Remember that men! (and some women!) Wow - I forgot what we were talking about. Oh the old times! Yeah, great stories for sure. Keep them coming...I enjoy reading them! We are lucky we live in the now though, know what I mean? Look at all we can play now! Think of all we've been through, and played through - the birth of video games! A lot of people aren't with us any longer that enjoyed video and computer games. We're the lucky ones! We made it! (We're still gaming!) Sorry, it's Sunday and someone's gotta preach...
