#4006. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

Bence "Beedyboy" Hamos reflects on 8 years at Crytek helping build Hunt: Showdown's community.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Hunt: Showdown community received a sucker punch in September when it learned that Bence "Beedyboy" Hamos, a beloved community-facing figure for the long-running extraction shooter, was unceremoniously let go in a wave of Crytek layoffs that affected at least 30 people.

For years Hamos was one of the faces of Hunt: Showdown, hosting livestreams, vlogs, and social media videos that kept players abreast of their favorite game's happenings. Through the highs and lows of Hunt's updates, events, and occasional controversies, he was a steady presence—calm, exuberant, and in touch with the experience of average players.

Hamos began at Crytek in 2018 in a social media role, eventually climbing to senior broadcast manager. As someone who absorbs the work of community managers constantly for work, I believe Hamos was particularly good at it—which is why his sudden departure hit Hunt's most dedicated players hard.

Hamos grew up in Budapest, Hungary. He'd looked up to Crytek since he was a teenager playing Crysis with his brother. He moved to Germany to find work and jumped at a job posting at the famed studio in 2018. He worked there for nearly nine years, focused entirely on Hunt: Showdown.

I caught up with Hamos last month, soon after his last day at Crytek, to learn what it was like to cultivate Hunt's community over nine years and talk about his unexpected departure.

"I really looked up to Crytek," Hamos told me. "[Getting hired] was such an unbelievable moment in my life, which obviously completely changed my whole career. It was nothing I never imagined I'd do. I was super happy."

Hamos said he had never worked in games when he interviewed at Crytek, but managed to charm the studio with his experience managing his rock band's social media, interacting with its community, and running livestreams on Ustream.

"It was right before the launch of Hunt, so in 2018," Hamos, who had recently moved to Germany from his home in Budapest to look for work, recounted. "I saw an opportunity at Crytek for a very entry-level social media position, and they really needed something.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"Somehow, by huge luck, I got hired in two weeks."

When Hamos arrived at Crytek in early 2018, the industry was in the middle of a major shift toward live service games. Fortnite had yet to become the biggest game in the world, battle passes didn't exist outside mobile and MOBAs, and Crytek was taking a big chance on an FPS format so early in its infancy that it didn't have an established name yet: the extraction shooter. There was no playbook for communications in a game that's always changing, so Hamos did what came naturally.

To deal with a community and manage a community, you have to be part of a community

"I always had this principle that to deal with a community and manage a community, you have to be part of a community. So that's why I played a bunch of Hunt," he said. "I played over 2,000 or 3,000 hours just in my personal account, not even my testing account. I streamed it in my personal time.

"I think it's super important in a position like that to not just understand what the company wants, and the vision for the company, but also the other side of the equation—what players are feeling. I would understand their frustration. I would see the issues firsthand."

Hamos says his extensive hours in Hunt put him in a sometimes "weird" position of representing the interests of both the players and devs, which did not always align.

"You're the voice of the community, and you have to push that to the dev team and let them know about feedback and issues people are talking about. But at the same time, you also push the vision of the team and answers to the community from the dev side. It's a weird mixture."

I was curious what that process actually looked like, behind the scenes. How would a community manager package up player sentiment and deliver it to devs who aren't as deeply embedded in Reddit or YouTube?

"So we would collect reports on a weekly or bi-weekly basis, depending on the time period, and we would have to actually measure and collect it. Like, 'Hey, this many players are positive about this subject. These are the mixed ones. These are the negative ones.' And we list them out and say '200 people are saying this is bad.' That's a high priority from the community side, and you want to look at different platforms too, like socials, Steam, Reddit, Discord, and even your personal DMs, because not everyone has an X or BlueSky account. Those are all counted in, but it has to be accurate."

Hamos also explained how being the go-between for players and devs sometimes means taking a popular idea to the team and getting a no.

"There may be things that the community is really asking for, but the team is definitely saying no to. Whatever the reason: It may be not in line with the vision of the game or simply technical reasons, it may take too much time, and you really have to prioritize things because live service games always need updates, and people always want the big shiny things," he said. "When that happens, you just have to be transparent with the community and not ignore it."

The other side of that coin is calibrating feedback (especially balance feedback) from platforms that are prone to hyperbole.

"When you talk about a game like Hunt, you have to understand that the vocal part of the community may be veteran players that have been playing for a long time, and may be the highest-skill six star players, but that's actually a minority of all players. So you cannot necessarily balance the game around 1% or even less than 1% of the player base when your numbers show that it's not actually a problem for the community," he said.

"If you're talking about balancing a weapon [for example], designers look at the percentage of people using it in every skill level. Sometimes it may look very loud on Reddit that, say, the weapon is way too overpowered, but when you look at the data, it may be actually a super low percentage of people using it. They would then decide to make a small change or even show the data to players.

You cannot necessarily balance the game around 1% or even less than 1% of the player base...

"It has happened before where we said, 'Hey guys, here's the usage rate, this is why we are not planning on changing it, and it's not actually as big of a deal as you may perceive it," he said. "I think the community appreciates it when they can see the numbers behind things."

But Hamos also offered an example of an adjustment made with high-skill players in mind that didn't really affect the rest of the community: Making Spitzer ammo, a special bullet type that increases bullet velocity, a scarce lootable item instead of something you can buy from the store whenever.

"Today, Hunt has so many layers and so much depth that you can really make small adjustments that may not affect lower-skill players," he said. " I always had a lot of trust and respect for the designers. They really know what they are doing, so I think Hunt and the community are in good hands in this regard."

Hamos had nothing but amazing things to say about his coworkers and experience working at Crytek, even if the way he left was, in his words, shocking and sad.

"It came out of nowhere. And after nine years, I did feel like a part of my soul was ripped out because it was my day-to-day. I kind of lived and breathed the game. I would wake up and think about Hunt and work on Hunt. It has been a part of my entire adult life, basically," he said. "So I was shocked and sad, and I'm still sad. I still get a bit emotional about it because it's painful, but I don't have any hard feelings."

His firing was part of a wider round of layoffs at Crytek, the second the studio has been through since February 2025. Hamos understands that the game industry is a "pretty rough space" right now, with tens of thousands of developers displaced in the last three years, and showed no sign of bitterness—in keeping with this jolly demeanor in countless Hunt update videos. On his last official day, Hamos posted a farewell message on the official Hunt subreddit—it quickly became the top post on the page with thousands of upvotes and hundreds of supportive comments. The response was "really special," as he recalled.

"To get faced with the fact that your work meant so much to people is something really special. I'm trying not to get emotional here, but when you work day-to-day, you don't really feel that. But now when it's over, it is kind of a payoff for all of that, which really hits like a truck," he said. "It's not something that I expected or maybe even deserved, but something that meant a lot to me."

Unlike countless colleagues now left in the lurch by layoffs, Hamos was fortunate enough to quickly land a new gig, thanks in large part to his recognizable community work on Hunt. In October, he became head of community and social at Good Fun Corporation, a studio formed by former Hell Let Loose developers. They're making Hunger: an old-timey extraction game with distinct similarities to Hunt.

It came out of nowhere. And after nine years, I did feel like a part of my soul was ripped out because it was my day-to-day. I kind of lived and breathed the game.

"Of course there are similar vibes to Hunt in Hunger, though it's an extraction RPG, which is very different. It has a lot of MMO elements to it and progression and questing, which appeals to me a lot."

Hamos is starting over from scratch, and his highest hope is to cultivate a community as friendly, passionate, and sturdy as Hunt: Showdown.

"I think [Hunt] is one of the least toxic communities. Of course there's some toxicity, but the people are more mature and understanding compared to most. And since it's a bit smaller overall, you also have this little family kind of vibe where we're talking to people who also understand the game and live the same hunter life."

Hamos told me the end of his time at Crytek doesn't mean the end of his own Hunt career. He still loves the game and believes its best days are ahead.

"Many games enter with a bang and then fade out quickly with fewer players unless they have a major update. Hunt, especially among live service shooters, is really an exception to the rule. You see growth forever—like it's still going," he said.

"I just wish the best for Hunt and hope it will stay for another 10 years at least."

#4003. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

#4002. Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3's online servers are temporarily going dark, FromSoftware announces

Things might get even darker over in the world of Lordran without those silly, only sometimes helpful notes left by other players. Developer FromSoftware has announced that it's temporarily closing Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers because of an unspecified issue.

"Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms," the RPG studio tweeted earlier today, before naming Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3.

While the server shutdown won't last forever, FromSoftware hasn't told series fans when exactly they can expect online play to be restored. That presumably means PvP invasions, summon signs and in-game messages that try to troll you off a cliff are unavailable for the time being.

"We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience," the studio added. I hope you've stocked up on Estus Flasks, at least.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

Pikachu Puppetronic is peak gift material

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Things move fast in the world of toys, but this Pikachu animatronic stole a place in our hearts and has stayed put ever since.

There are so many reasons this little guy won over Pokémon fans when it was first unveiled at New York Toy Fair earlier this year. For starters, 'Pikachu Puppetronic' is utterly adorable, very close to real-size, and captures the pocket-monster's distinctive look surprisingly well. But it's also crammed with so many extra features, including over 120 unique animations and numerous sounds. Considering how it's normally $80 (and is now significantly less thanks to a 40% price cut at Amazon), it's surprisingly good value.

This is a record-low price for the Pikachu Puppetronic figure, and for most of its shelf life it's remained stubbornly at full price or $ 78-ish. That makes this offer an absolute steal, and I'd be surprised if we saw anything more generous come the Black Friday sale.

In terms of what it can do, this Pokémon is pretty tricked out; alongside sound and lighting effects (like light-up cheeks), it has three sensors for motion-activated interactions in the nose, head, and tummy. It also has a moving mouth and dual-motion ears. When you throw in those 120+ unique animations, Pikachu Puppetronic feels surprisingly lifelike in motion.

As for the name, it references how this is a cross between a puppet and a traditional animatronic. While it moves like a traditional animatronic, it's controlled like a puppet. This is done via a subtle slit in the back, and it's hard to see from the front – further selling the illusion.

Besides being a really neat collectible for fans, this is also peak gifting material – and I suspect that discount will make it all the more tempting.

#4000. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#3999. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

Queen's Domain might be the trendy game of the moment but for my money, the classic grid-based action of Underkeep is where it's at. (And yes, there's a demo.)

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Everyone's talking about Queen's Domain right now, but as someone who tried Queen's Domain and did not care for it, allow me to direct your attention to an alternative old-school dungeon crawler: Underkeep, which launched on Steam on November 5 and has been absolutely phenomenal through the roughly four hours I've put into it so far.

Like Queen's Domain, Underkeep is firmly rooted in the 1990s, but I'm talkin' the early '90s, and even before that: Classic grid-based RPGs like The Bard's Tale, Dungeon Master, Wizardry, and Eye of the Beholder. In fact, as someone who loves Eye of the Beholder (specifically the second one, The Legend of Darkmoon), I noticed a lot of nearly direct lifts from that series: primarily visual, but also a few audio cues, that I swear I've heard before.

But my concerns that Underkeep might be a low-effort knockoff evaporated pretty quickly. After four hours of play I feel like I've barely scratched the game's surface: I still haven't found the titular village of Underkeep, where I assume the real action will begin, but I've crashed (literally, in a few cases) through multiple dungeons, all interconnected horizontally or vertically, and explored an overworld that's a whole lot bigger than I expected. At the very least, Underkeep looks beefy.

Underkeep's gameplay preserves the vibe of those old-time RPGs while eliminating most of their more objectionable nonsense. Its shared inventory is divided into categories that make managing and swapping equipment between party members extremely easy, the automapping is detailed while still allowing freehand notes (I know, I know, get some paper and do your own maps, but who has time for that these days?), and tools are used automatically without needing to be equipped.

And unlike so many games in the genre, Underkeep is entirely turn-based. This eliminates the cheese strategy of hitting an enemy and moving a step away before they can hit back, which carried so many gamers through so many fights in so many games over the years. But it also encourages more thoughtfulness: When I see an enemy in the distance, I can take my time to think about what I want to do, move to a more advantageous position, or even just go take a break for a while.

I'm free to do whatever I want until melee combat actually begins. Once that happens, everyone in the party has to finish their turn, and then let the enemies finish theirs, at which point we're all free to run away (and probably be chased) or launch another round of fighting. I'll always come down on the real-time-with-pause side of the argument for isometric RPGs, but the turn-based approach is ideal for Underkeep.

Character classes are a fairly standard mix—fighter, paladin, wizard, thief, that sort of thing—but the races are a bit more interesting. Humans and dwarves are on the menu, and "elk" are kind of like elves, but then you get the stoneborn, raven, and slugman, all of them nicely weird. Stoneborn, for instance, are basically golems⁠—extremely strong and tough, but they have the agility of a Mack truck and can't wear body armor. They're basically a boulder that can hit you really hard, which is great in some ways but has some real drawbacks too. Ravens, meanwhile, are subject to random mutations that can take them off in unforeseeable directions: My own raven character recently mutated a healing buff called Roommate from the Void: "Something moved into your body at some point and never left. It pays rent in blood."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Slugmen, well, they're just slugs who are also men. They look like this:

There's also no limit to combining races and classes: A stoneborn thief or slugman paladin may not be a great idea, but if you want to give it a shot, knock yourself out.

There's not a lot of reading to do in Underkeep, but the writing for those encounters is pleasingly evocative in an old-school tabletop way, and there are plenty of surprises to be had too. Depending on how you deal with the red-cloaked guy above, for instance, you may get a reward, you might get jumped, or you could find yourself facing some sort of bigger trouble down the road—that's not confirmed yet, but I definitely got some 'Be seein' you' stinkeye from him before he slunk off into the next life.

It makes me a little sad to say, but one of my first thoughts when I saw Underkeep was whether the assets were made with generative AI. I'm not the only one to have that worry: Multiple arguments about it are underway in the Steam forums right now. Unlike some people in those conversations who say they "can just tell" when AI is present, I cannot—but the Steam store page has no AI disclosure, and developer Rake in Grass has repeatedly insisted that no generative AI was used.

"All artwork in Underkeep was hand-drawn by our artists," an FAQ states. "Some variations in style are natural, as several artists contributed to the game. The occasional "mixels" are caused by dynamic scaling used to simulate 3D perspective and smooth animations."

It's unfortunate that debates like this are so commonplace now, because Underkeep is a joy: I haven't played a whole huge lot of them in recent years, but this is easily my favorite grid-based RPG since the great Legend of Grimrock 2, which is now 12 years old. (Quick correction: The original Grimrock will soon be 15, Grimrock 2 isn't quite there yet. Thanks to Sebastian for letting me know.)

Underkeep is out now on Steam for $19.50, a 15% launch discount on the regular price that's available until November 19. You can also sample the goods by way of the demo, which offers about an hour of highly compressed gameplay and some fun surprises.

We won't know how well GTA 6 is selling during its pre-order phase until after the game's launch next week, but with the biggest entertainment release of all time projected and now Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick talking up the numbers, we could be looking at some absurd sales stats.

Speaking alongside the publication of financial reports, Zelnick said GTA 6 pre-orders are "running far in excess of our expectations". The game has been available to pre-order 25th June 2026, so they'll have been available for almost five months when GTA 6 finally comes out on 19th November. That's a long time to build up millions of pre-orders.

"That’s a good thing. That said, we never claim success before it occurs,” Zelnick continued when talking to Variety. “So we’re just days away from beginning to see the fruits of our labour."

#3996. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#3995. GOTY hopeful Mina the Hollower bought the studio financial stability "for now," while the Shovel Knight devs work on a new 3D game

Yacht Club Games has confirmed that most of its developers are now working on a brand new 3D game (potentially Shovel Knight 3D), after the critically-acclaimed Mina the Hollower did well enough for the team to continue.

Before launching its old-school adventure game earlier this year, Yacht Club described Mina the Hollower as a "make-or-break" moment for the beloved indie studio. A global pandemic and a failed experiment to turn Yacht Club into a multi-project studio had left the developer on thin ice, it seems.

But Mina the Hollower sold well enough to buy the studio more time, according to a new Reddit AMA full of interesting tidbits. Asked if Mina was able to secure financial stability for the company, Sean Velasco simply said "yes… for now!" Mina managed to sell over 500,000 copies in its first two weeks, so it's well on its way to the one million copies the devs were once hoping for.

For the foreseeable future, the devs aren't ready to talk about the kinds of DLC and spin-offs and follow-ups that dear old Shovel Knight enjoyed for many years, but they're not abandoning their newest baby either. "We're working on more post-release features," the devs wrote, which includes "expanded randomizer options, enemy and boss randomization, more modifiers, speedrunner features" and more ways "to do even more in Mina."

Another fan also asked the folks at Yacht Club about their unannounced 3D Shovel Knight game - Velasco previously told Bloomberg that the game was halfway done before the entire studio put all hands on deck for Mina, and pivoted back into a one-game outfit. Alec Faulkner stopped short of confirming Shovel Knight 3D, but said "most of us are currently working on a 3D game, yes!" Alright then, Alec, keep your secrets. "Not sayin more! Other than that it’s gonna be soooooooo awesome."

Co-founder Nick Wozniac went further into the state of the developer, and why splitting the team in half was probably a mistake. Here's what he had to say on the matter: "Sales are the things that keep the company afloat so it's not born from greed (mostly) that we say we'd love to see more sales, it's all about continuing to work together and make great games and reaping the rewards along the way. We are doing ok and learned a lot this cycle. I think we learned mostly that keeping the team tight and focused is what helped Mina land. Splitting the team up to work on two games was something we could have corrected a long time ago but I'm glad to be where we are now. Just gotta pocket those lessons and use them to drive you forward."

Eurogamer's five-star Mina the Hollower review called it an "adventure that takes inspiration from the greats."

Today during ExileCon's keynote address Grinding Gear Games announced that Path of Exile 2's full release on December 11 will bring not one, but two new classes: Alongside the previously announced Duelist, 1.0 will also introduce the dagger-heavy, trap-wielding Shadow, capable of employing a suite of new stealth mechanics.

The Shadow's addition had been hinted at with a cryptic teaser trailer, which you can see here. The class's inclusion is welcome news to those of us—like yours truly—who very much enjoy playing these sneaky stabbers. On release, Shadows will be able to ascend as the returning Assassin, or choose a new ascendancy: the Infiltrator.

We know that eventually, every PoE2 character class will have (at least) three ascendancies. Whether the Shadow's third will be the Saboteur, the Trickster, or something new like the Sorceress's Disciple of Varashta is yet to be seen.

As has been the case with previous PoE 2 class additions, the Shadow's arrival will also introduce a new weapon type and abilities. In 1.0, alongside the Duelist's swords, we'll also be getting the dagger, and with it all new skill gems and supports. We should see an absolute explosion of playstyle archetypes on top of PoE2's already healthy build diversity.

The Shadow will introduce new mechanics like stealth, which prevents monsters from seeing you until you’re close by. It has a cooldown, but since it’s reset on kill, you should be able to use it to kill quickly from the shadows and get moving again.

Stealth interacts with the Shadow's returning trap skills, too. While PoE 1 traps were mostly just hucked at monsters' feet mid-combat, traps thrown from stealth in PoE 2 won't trigger until you reveal yourself, giving an actual feel of pulling off an ambush, There will be eight different trap types in 1.0, all of which interact with each other in unique ways.

There is, as ever is the case with Path of Exile, even more. When entering stealth, you leave behind a shade that blinds monsters and acts as a distraction. Your shade will also copy melee attacks you use, doubling up on your damage. And Shadows will be able to utilize a new Darkness resource, which can be collected from darkness-spreading skills to buff the damage you deal when emerging from stealth.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

We’ll know more about these classes later, but between all these new abilities and ascendancies as well as two new acts, a new league, and endgame improvements Path of Exile 2’s full release is looking absolutely stacked.

#3992. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.

#3991. A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

#3989. Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic's next DLC is set to expand the city building sim into the one place not corrupted by capitalism: SPACE

Following not the inherent liberal capitalistic framework of city builders like SimCity but instead a revolutionary (sorry) interpretation of planning and logistical simulation that prioritises centralisation and minute detail, Hooded Horse and 3DIVISION's Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic offers a tense, socialist look at what a citybuilder could be. Fellow contributor Sin Vega, in her 1.0 review, described it like this: "You have to build things to demolish things. That might be Workers & Resources in a nutshell. You're not managing budgets (money is exclusively for imports/exports), you're organising stuff." Now, having previously expanding out of the Soviet Republic and across the globe with the World Maps DLC, the next step for socialist citybuilding is, of course, space. Our Edwin outright predicted this two years ago, correctly calling that "the logical endgame here is to go to space." Good on him.

The Space Program DLC, set to release on November 23rd, will add a variety of new technologies and types of industry to the builder. It looks like it'll focus on not only the actual rockets that get into space, and the spectacle of it all, but also the huge amounts of science and industry that get to the point of rockets not exploding upon takeoff. For example, while it's all well and good for Space Program's scientists to be able to design rockets that are capable of remaining together for long enough to land safely, the designs they dream of still have to be built, meaning that industrial pipelines must be effectively centralised to ensure that every single component is of high quality and arriving in the required quantity.

The update also specifies the Sputnik and Vostok programs as elements of the expansion, implying a close historical aspect to it — though, elsewhere, "an unprecedented duel with nature" is mentioned, which is referring to either the simple harshness of space or aliens. Jury's out. A 1960s campaign will be a star feature of the DLC, which is described as a place for players to learn the new mechanics "in relative peace, surrounded by a happy, healthy, and economically stable utopia." What an idea.

#3988. Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update

Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.

Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.

SILENT HILL: TownfallNotice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.*The PlayStation®5 version is…

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.

PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.

To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. Matt said Townfall showed Silent Hill's "stellar revival continues as new developer Screen Burn melds stealth, meticulous world design, and a dash of social realism for a different sort of survival horror", and awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review.

Two factions of gamers and game developers are at an impasse.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kenney, an artist known for giving away thousands of free game assets, did not expect to wind up directly arguing with specific billionaires after telling off billionaires in general in a recent X post. But a few hours after he encouraged other artists not to give in to pressure to use generative AI, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney was in his replies.

"This is bullshit, Kenney," Sweeney told the artist, concluding his rebuttal with a cute double entendre: "I've upped my expectations of AI. Up yours!"

Richest-person-in-the-world Elon Musk also chimed in to back up Sweeney. Hundreds of other comments on the exchange inevitably followed, spanning the full spectrum of AI opinions.

Kenney's contentious post was: "Don't let billionaires convince you slop is the future. They're used to managing & directing, not making things themselves. Of course they can't see the difference. They don't understand your love for the craft. Keep making personal, beautiful games. You've got my support 💖"

The artist had not had Sweeney in mind when he wrote the post; it was a response to something Musk had said. Kenney expected it to be read by other artists who may feel pressured to use generative AI despite objecting to it.

"I think AI has some benefit but there's just too many problems with it that I find it immoral to use in its current state," Kenney told PC Gamer in a chat after that exchange. "Whether it's the environmental issues, data centers, theft during training, or the negative impact it has on pretty much every industry."

Sweeney is not known to keep his opinions to himself, but the Epic CEO has been particularly active in his defense of generative AI on X recently.

As a provider of technology to the whole industry, I see it as Epic's job and my job to make the positive case for it.

While some companies use AI but stay quiet about it—Baldur's Gate 3 developer Larian received substantial pushback for discussing limited AI use last year, as an example of how the conversation can go—Epic has made its support for AI tools unambiguous. The company is going "all-in" on AI-assisted game development with its next Unreal Engine release, proudly calls the new version of its Epic Games Store launcher "vibe coded," and recently announced an AI-focused game jam.

Meanwhile, Sweeney has joined likeminded X users in battling what they see as online persecution from an anti-AI "hate mob."

"Because speaking in favor of AI draws such harsh criticism, there is great reluctance among most professional AI adopters in gaming to speak up," the Epic CEO told PC Gamer this week. "As a provider of technology to the whole industry, I see it as Epic's job and my job to make the positive case for it."

According to Sweeney, opposition to AI in games is not a popular view. He has described the anti-AI crowd as "a pessimistic minority running a venomous, vocal pressure campaign to force compliance and silence dissent," and claimed this week that most opposition to AI comes from "astroturfed anti-AI influence campaigns."

PC Gamer has not seen any evidence for that last claim, but it is the case that "AI slop" accusations on social media have not been matched by a massive rejection of AI from the broader gaming audience.

The generative AI use in Arc Raiders led to a 2/5 review in Eurogamer, but the extraction shooter nevertheless sold over 16 million copies. Several games on Steam's current top sellers list also disclose AI use, including Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Aion 4, MapleStory, and indie game Moon Sweepers, which just announced 600,000 sales.

A recent survey of Steam users by GameDiscoverCo found that the majority, about 69%, are either "neutral," "fine with," or "have absolutely no problem with" buying games that disclose the use of AI in their development, something Steam requires for certain applications of AI.

However, the survey found that the disclosures themselves are popular. According to its results, most Steam users check them before buying a game, and over 55% of respondents think Steam should have even stricter AI disclosure rules.

Sweeney is staunchly against Steam's disclosure requirement, calling it "abhorrent" and claiming that it forces developers to make a political statement that incites "cancel campaigns and public struggle sessions" against them.

Kenney's read on the situation is the opposite of Sweeney's: that a minority which includes billionaire tech executives is pushing hard to normalize generative AI tools and get everyone hooked on them despite resistance from a public that wants to see "soul and love put into games."

"If it were true and AI has had mass adoption, why even bother going after me or trying to convince me to start using it?" Kenney asks.

"I'd rather leave the industry someday when I'm old(...er) and have everyone remember me for the good stuff I did and the many people I've helped, rather than for lining my own pockets.

Some gamers do support the use of AI—or, as established, are at least willing to accept the use of generative AI tools—but even as OpenAI boasts over a billion monthly active users, it's easy to find people who share Kenney's total distaste of AI, and the conversation is not limited to mean X posts.

As of the most recent Game Developers Conference survey, over 50% of devs think AI is bad for the industry. Wariness of data centers crosses party lines in the US, as we just saw in the midterm elections. A large survey of PC Gamer readers recently came back strongly against generative AI in games.

One developer went so far as to cancel their Epic Games Store release in support of Kenney. "We just don't wanna be associated with such an embarrassing platform," said the studio, Dead Teapot.

Kenney is a particularly appropriate figure for the anti-AI game development crowd to rally around, embodying the communal, cooperative artmaking spirit that big AI is seen to threaten. For over a decade, Kenney has been releasing free assets for game developers. It started with leftover art from abandoned Flash game projects, and now the artist makes a living from donations, as well as sales of a $20 bundle that packages all 60,000 assets into one download.

"It isn't a lot, which isn't too surprising if you give nearly everything away for free, but it's enough to [get] by," says Kenney. "I'd rather leave the industry someday when I'm old(...er) and have everyone remember me for the good stuff I did and the many people I've helped, rather than for lining my own pockets."

Meanwhile, Sweeney argues that productivity-aids like generative AI are necessary to make game development economically viable today. He recently reposted an AI-generated cartoon depicting a dev's game launch being ruined by an angry anti-AI mob after they used AI to cut their costs, claiming: "This is exactly what's happening."

I'm worried that the part of the industry I love is going to disappear or be taken over by people who aren't in it for the love of the craft, but rather for the grift.

In the back-and-forth that followed Sweeney's rebuttal to Kenney's "don't let billionaires convince you slop is the future" post, the Epic CEO told Kenney that his reason for pushing back is that "there's risk that convincing devs to abstain from the new way leaves them behind."

"I'm concerned that development studios swept up in these anti-AI campaigns will make decisions that render themselves uncompetitive in the global market for games," Sweeney told PC Gamer this week. He predicts that studios will see "productivity gains of at least 2x to 4x" with AI tools, and says that "all developers need to be prepared for this."

For Kenney and likeminded developers and players, however, a game development scene that's all-in on generative AI would not be a more efficient continuation of the same scene they helped build, but a betrayal of it—something they fundamentally don't want to be a part of.

"I'm not worried about myself or my own studio," says Kenney. "I'm worried that the part of the industry I love is going to disappear or be taken over by people who aren't in it for the love of the craft, but rather for the grift."

And regarding the concern that developers who don't embrace AI will be left behind: "Please, leave me behind," says Kenney. "I'm pretty happy here."

Tyler grew up in Silicon Valley during the '80s and '90s, playing games like Zork and Arkanoid on early PCs. He was later captivated by Myst, SimCity, Civilization, Command & Conquer, all the shooters they call "boomer shooters" now, and PS1 classic Bushido Blade (that's right: he had Bleem!). Tyler joined PC Gamer in 2011, and today he's focused on the site's news coverage. His hobbies include amateur boxing and adding to his 1,200-plus hours in Rocket League.

#3986. I'm sad that the Like A Dragon creator's new studio is closing, but I wish their now-cancelled debut Gang of Dragon wasn't just LAD again

Less than a year after the announcement of their first game, and only four years after the studio's creation, Gang of Dragon developers Nagoshi Studio have been dissolved by a shareholders' resolution (thanks, Gematsu.) That also means a premature end for Gang of Dragon, which was announced at last year's Game Awards with a flashy trailer featuring Like a Dragon-esque realistic visuals, combat and exploration through Kabukicho, a couple new elements like actual gunplay and car chases, as well as the star power of actor Ma Dong-seok (a.k.a. Don Lee). Following reports in March that NetEase, the studio's source of funding, would be pulling said funding in May due to ballooning costs reaching around seven billion yen, the time has sadly come for Nagoshi Studio, having not found any alternative funding sources in the time since.

Gang of Dragon looked very much to be 'just Like a Dragon again', which I find to be something of a depressing fate for a studio headed by the original series' creator. Having left Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio following Judgment and Yakuza: Like a Dragon, two of its most innovative games both with new protagonists and one entirely new turn-based gameplay style, it feels indicative of the industry that Nagoshi was granted funding seemingly on the condition that the studio makes something that just looks like the rest of the Like a Dragon series. I love Ma Dong-seok as an actor, but his presence was one of the more blatant, 'look, we got that guy!' castings of the LAD archetype, which is saying something considering Infinite Wealth had fucking Danny Trejo in a prominent role. The trailer closing with a shot of Dong-seok framed by Kabukicho's torii gate, maybe the most famous image from the Like a Dragon series, put a sour taste in my mouth as being just more of the same brand recognition (yet, for a new IP!) to prioritise safe return on investment.

I'm unfortunately not that surprised to see Gang of Dragon and Nagoshi Studio lost to time, though I am sad about it. I have some conflicted feelings on Nagoshi as a person/auteur, but I don't think he, or his studio, deserves to have funding pulled before they could even release anything as a result of NetEase deciding to pull investments out of non-Chinese companies over time. It's unknown what Nagoshi and the team will be attempting next, but I truly hope they can eventually make something. No More Heroes studio Grasshopper Manufacture was able to detach themselves from NetEase very recently and possibly avoid a similar fate, so it might not be impossible.

#3985. Final Fantasy 14 reveals Evercold’s second new job and February release date, with pre-orders opening next week

Plus Square Enix confirms Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35m registered accounts.

Final Fantasy 14's next expansion, Evercold, will launch on 23rd February 2027, and its second new job is zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that fights with a crossbow and a bird.

Producer and director Naoki Yoshida revealed the job during the opening keynote of the Final Fantasy 14 Fan Festival 2026 in Tokyo. Zephyr pairs crossbow shots with support from an avian familiar called Nephele, and joins Bastion, the greatshield-wielding tank revealed as Evercold's first new job at Fan Festival Berlin earlier this year.

Pre-orders for Evercold and the previously announced Collector's Box open on Wednesday 4th November at 9am GMT. Anyone who pre-orders gets early access, plus a Wind-Up Köttr minion and Halone's Earring, which boosts EXP from defeating enemies by 30 percent. The in-game items are delivered as soon as you pre-order, so you can use the earring to level jobs before Evercold arrives.

The Collector's Box is physical goods only. It doesn't include the game, in-game items or pre-order bonuses. Inside you'll find an art box featuring an Evercold illustration by Yoshitaka Amano, a figure of the Warrior of Light as a reaper, an Ethos metal keychain, a Köttr mini plush, and a Tapestry of the Fourth.

The Square Enix Store is also selling a limited Collector's Bundle that pairs the box with a code for the Digital Collector's Edition on Windows or Mac. Players on PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and Steam can buy the box on its own and pre-order the Digital Collector's Edition separately. The digital edition adds a Valhallar Odin mount, an Entreat Crystal emote, and a Crystal Skyltborg weapon for Bastion.

Square Enix also used the keynote to reveal a new Fierce raid difficulty, sitting between Normal and Savage; a new trailer for the Evangelion: Ghosts of Desire alliance raid crossover, plus tougher eight-player battles built around some of its bosses; and new Tetsuya Nomura artwork for Beyond the Lifestream, a raid series crossover with the Final Fantasy 7 Remake series.

We can also expect Evolved Combat Mode, which Square Enix says highlights each job's unique identity; Seasons, a new system that changes how item rewards are earned; and expanded character creation with new Character Action Skins. Expanded housing features, PvP updates, and a revamped companion chocobo system will follow from patch 8.1.

Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35 million registered accounts.

You can watch the full keynote on Twitch, and there's more on the official Evercold site.

Final Fantasy 14 is now available on Switch 2. The port was announced at the end of June.

#3984. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser all but confirms Hammerfell setting and means we can finally stop using that eight year old header image with the hills

Say hello to sandy scroll screengrab for the foreseeable future

Praise Talos and whatever other Elder Scrolls deities you might worship. We here at RPS and in the wider gaming press finally have new material to use when hunting for images to symbolise The Elder Scrolls 6. No more will we be limited to that shot of some hills from the 2018 teaser, because Bethesda have shown off an elder scroll covered in sand while revealing the new game's subtitle and all but locking in a setting. As a recent report from The Verge claimed, it's called The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel and looks to be set in Hammerfell.

These details were revealed in a short teaser at the end of a Todd Howard-fronted video celebrating Bethesda Game Studios' 40th anniversary. As such, the majority of the video is the Toddinator recapping the studio's history by touching on each of the games they've put out since 1986's Gridiron. Then, he looks to the future. "You know, everybody’s always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," the Toddfather said. "And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

Cue a shot of an elder scroll buried in sand, followed by the The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel in fancy logo font. Then, a quote attributed to a moth priest called Yazar. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." OOH, CRYPTIC. In all seriousness, between the subtitle, the sand, and Yazar being referred to as a moth priest in service of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, the Verge report's assertion that the game will be set in Hammerfell is essentially set in stone by this teaser even if his Toddliness didn't spell it out himself.

Sentinel's the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. The inclusion of an elder scroll in the teaser and the quote from Yazar also lend credence to the Verge report's claim that the game will make a big thing out of unravelling secrets linked to the provenance of these mysterious bits of paper. As for the quote's yammering of lost futures and undone victories, I'll venture to speculate that it could turn out to be reference to the player character thwarting a Thalmor victory, since Skyrim seemed to set up the elves as being on the verge of conquering Tamriel as the Cyrodillic empire fractured and fell.

That may or may not be the case, but we do know for sure that this teaser likely means a huge downturn in use of the header image below. It's eight years old, pulled from The Elder Scrolls 6's infamous 2018 teaser. All these years on, the game's finally on the way. You've served us well, screengrab of some hills. Talos guide you to wherever less regularly used images go.

Elder Scrolls teasing aside, it's worth bearing in mind that Bethesda parent company Microsoft have spent the majority of this year gutting their workforce with mass layoffs and studio ditching. Microsoft are also still currently subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#3983. Activision to remove Itaewon crowd crush footage from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and apologises to victims' families

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims."

Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

In a new statement reported by Inven Global, Activision said the footage "will be completely removed" via a game update scheduled to roll out on 12th November.

The statement was issued in Korean, and the quotes come via Inven Global's AI-assisted, editor-reviewed translation.

As we reported earlier this week, the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died. The bereaved families' association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting called for its removal.

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims who were deeply hurt by this incident, as well as to everyone we have caused concern," Activision said.

The publisher also said that Modern Warfare 4 "is a work of fiction created to provide realistic immersion", and it "never intended to evoke or trivialise any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush" by using real news broadcast footage.

The controversy has also reached the South Korean government. During a press briefing, minister of the interior and safety Yun Ho-jung described the footage's inclusion as "secondary harm", and said: "I believe appropriate sanctions should be imposed".

"Using such a tragedy as material for a game, a form of entertainment or business, is something that should be refrained from as a matter of human ethics," Yun added. He said it was up to the relevant agencies to decide "whether to impose punishment or block it to make general access difficult".

Activision's earlier statement to Eurogamer said the opening cinematic "utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative", and was "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

Grand Theft Auto 6 finally arrives on November 19, but not for us, no—the big day is only for gamers on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. We're not being completely excluded, though: We can't have GTA 6 in November, but we can take advantage of pre-release discounts on a bunch of older GTA games—deals that, ironically, don't appear to be available on consoles.

As noted by GamesRadar, there are four GTA games available in two releases: Grand Theft Auto 3, Vice City, and San Andreas bundled up in the GTA Trilogy for $19.79/£19.79/€19.79—67% off the regular price—and Grand Theft Auto 4: Complete Edition, which includes The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony expansions, for $6/£5.09/€6, a 70% discount.

Those aren't the deepest discounts ever seen, but Grand Theft Auto games typically don't venture into the 90% off territory we all enjoy so much—and according to Isthereanydeal.com, this is as low as the GTA Trilogy has ever gone, and close to the mark for GTA 4.

You may recall that the GTA Trilogy Definitive Edition was a mess when it launched in 2021, but it seems to have turned that frown upside-down since then: On Steam, where the trilogy arrived in 2023, Vice City and San Andreas both hold "very positive" ratings. GTA 3 is stuck at a "mixed" rating, which is unfortunate: Glancing at user reviews, it sounds like the game still isn't in perfect shape, but it's also suffering from the fact that it's 25 years old, and was the first 3D game in the series—some jank and roughness was there right from the start.

Grand Theft Auto 4: The Complete Edition, on the other hand, doesn't suffer from those shortcomings. It's getting pretty long in the tooth too—it came out in 2008—but represents a shift in design and tone that led the series into what it is today. If you're looking for just one older GTA game to horse around with, this is the one, especially given that it's less than half the cost of the trilogy.

As mentioned, these sale prices are currently only being offered on Steam: There's currently no sign of any of them on either the Xbox or PlayStation stores (Fun fact: there actually is no digital version of GTA 4 on the PS Store because Sony didn't start selling full-priced games online until well after 2008). Maybe it's just coincidence, but they do appear to be intentional pre-GTA 6 sales: The discounts are on until November 19, when Grand Theft Auto 6 launches—except on PC.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. #3981. PUBG live-action series in the works at Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct and star

PUBG is being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Krafton announced the adaptation on 30th October, adding that Glover's brother Stephen, his writing partner on Atlanta, will join the project as a writer and executive producer.

The series will also be executive produced by Michael Schaefer for Neon TV, Fam Udeorji for Gilga, and Taeseok Jang and Sujin Lee for LV3H. LV3H is Krafton's entertainment arm, and it's involved in both developing and producing the show.

There's no word yet on a release window, plot, or who else will star.

Glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and says the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

Earlier this month, Krafton revealed it was ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago. The publisher’s other games include Subnautica and InZoi.

#3980. Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3 has been announced, marking another attempt at a free-to-play team game after Gundam Evolution's unfortunate fate

Bandai Namco have released the initial announcement trailer for Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3, a free-to-play team action game and a sequel to 2018's Battle Operation 2. The trailer is very, very pretty, showing off Gundam units clashing in large-scale battles and infantry fighting beneath the colossal mechas' feet (kinda like Titanfall, in having both human and mecha players in the same match). I'm sadly not yet enough of a true Gundam fan to recognise many of these units on sight other than the RX-78-2, but there's a real variety shown off here.

MOBILE SUIT GUNDAM GUNDAM BATTLE OPERATION 3　Announcement Trailer Watch on YouTube

While there's no release date specified in the trailer, Bandai Namco have confirmed that there will be a network test in Japan through November 20th-22nd, with an open network test planned for the future (thanks, Gematsu).

Following the fate of Gundam Evolution, a 2022 attempt at a hero shooter featuring Gundam units, it's nice to see another shot at taking the Gundam series into a team format. Evolution suffered from the all-too-common trappings of heavy microtransaction inclusion, with several playable Gundam units with unique abilities only available through paying real cash. It was rightly criticised for this, and since Bandai Namco seemed to have had high hopes for the revenue it could make from said microtransactions, the lack of money made meant it shut down just a year later.

Contrastingly, from what I can see, Gundam Battle Operation 2 was received fairly well on its release. While little is actually known about the third game at this point, let's hope it has a better chance than the series' last big release. I will quickly note that the trailer does close with a "*Some content may require purchase" note, so it'll likely have some form of microtransaction in itself — hopefully not to the same degree as Evolution. And, while we're on the topic of Gundam, there's also 2027's Gundam Rogue Orbit, a drastically different game that seems closer to a Devil May Cry-esque action title (though, unlike Battle Operation 3, will begin life as a timed exclusive to PS5). Now, if we could get a Gundam game that plays something like Armored Core, and god willing a proper PC release, I would be a very happy girl.
